chief_complaint: sudden shoulder weakness and pain after lifting heavy weight
hpi_details: 23M with sudden shoulder pain and weakness after lifting a heavy weight; assess active/passive motion, deformity, and distal neurovascular function while considering rotator cuff or biceps injury and dislocation.
ideas: He thinks he tore a muscle or ripped a ligament in his shoulder while lifting a heavy barbell at the gym.
concerns: He is worried that he permanently damaged his shoulder strength and will need invasive surgery to fix it.
expectations: He hopes to get an MRI to see how badly the muscle is torn and receive a referral to an orthopedic specialist.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute rotator cuff tear evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute rotator cuff tear is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Acute Rotator Cuff Tear: Shoulder MRI, refer to orthopedics for surgical repair, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden shoulder weakness and pain after lifting heavy weight

Key HPI features: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden shoulder weakness and pain after lifting heavy weight. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Rotator Cuff Tear.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute rotator cuff tear.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rotator cuff tendinopathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden weakness with a specific lifting event suggests acute tear rather than chronic tendinopathy.
management_principles: Plan for Acute Rotator Cuff Tear: Shoulder MRI, refer to orthopedics for surgical repair
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden shoulder weakness and pain after lifting heavy weight

A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden shoulder weakness and pain after lifting heavy weight. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Rotator Cuff Tear.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Acute Rotator Cuff Tear.
reference_soap.plan: Assess for deformity, fracture/dislocation, and distal neurovascular compromise; obtain radiographs when indicated, then MRI or ultrasound when it will clarify a suspected cuff tear. Provide analgesia and activity protection as appropriate. Refer promptly to orthopedics for substantial acute weakness or a confirmed traumatic full-thickness tear; operative versus nonoperative treatment depends on findings, function, and patient goals.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Rotator Cuff Tear
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Rotator Cuff Tear
Implement evidence-based management plan: Shoulder MRI, refer to orthopedics for surgical repair

teaching.one_liner: Patient with sudden shoulder weakness and pain after lifting a heavy weight, suggestive of tendon rupture.
red_flags: Sudden weakness with a specific lifting event suggests acute tear rather than chronic tendinopathy

must_ask.say: Can you describe exactly what you were lifting and how the pain started?
Do you feel true weakness lifting your arm, or is it mainly limited by pain?
Have you had any shoulder issues before this injury?
How is this affecting your daily activities or work?

must_ask.objective: Explain the MRI and surgical referral plan
must_ask.say: After checking for dislocation or fracture, imaging can clarify a tendon tear. An orthopedic specialist can discuss whether rehabilitation or repair best fits the findings and your goals.

history.answer: I was lifting a heavy barbell at the gym two days ago when I felt a sudden snap in my right shoulder, and now it hurts and feels completely weak.
It is only in my right shoulder, around the top and outer side. My left shoulder feels completely fine.
It started abruptly two days ago during my workout and has been bothering me constantly since then.
It is a sharp, tearing pain whenever I try to lift my arm, and a dull ache at rest that is about a 6 out of 10.
No, I have not noticed any swelling, redness, or heat in the shoulder joint.
I don't have morning stiffness in my joints, though the shoulder feels stiff when I wake up because I tried not to move it.
Trying to raise my arm out to the side or lift anything makes it worse, while resting it against my chest helps ease the pain.
I cannot lift my arm to put on a jacket or reach high shelves, and I am unable to lift items at work.
No, I haven't had any fever or chills.
Yes, I was doing an overhead shoulder press with a heavy barbell when I felt a sudden pop and my arm gave out immediately.
No, I have never had any shoulder dislocations, pain, or injuries before this.
I haven't had unexplained weight loss or fever, but I've been feeling worn down and fatigued because the pain makes it hard to sleep.
No, I do not have any skin rashes, mouth ulcers, hair thinning, red eyes, or dry eyes and mouth.
No, I don't have morning back pain, heel pain, or swollen fingers or toes.
No, I haven't had any recent diarrhea, burning urination, discharge, or sore throat.
I eat a standard diet without binging on meat or shellfish, and I don't take water pills.
No, I have never had steroid injections, shoulder operations, or artificial joint surgery, and I don't take immune-suppressing drugs.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my girlfriend and have no other sexual partners.
It is true weakness. Even when the pain is dull, I physically cannot keep my arm raised up on my own.
I think I tore a muscle or ripped a ligament when I was lifting heavy weights at the gym.
I'm really worried that I permanently ruined my shoulder and that I'll have to get surgery to fix it.
I'm hoping to get an MRI to see what tore in there and get referred to a specialist.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not on any prescription medications. I took some over-the-counter ibuprofen yesterday, which only slightly helped the ache.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink alcohol socially, about one or two beers on the weekend.
I work in a warehouse moving boxes and live in an apartment with a roommate.
My parents and siblings are healthy, with no history of joint disorders or arthritis.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert young male sitting comfortably, protectively holding his right arm against his side, without acute respiratory distress.

No deformity, ecchymosis, or swelling in either shoulder, with localized tenderness over the right greater tuberosity and subacromial space; passive range of motion is full, but active abduction and external rotation are markedly restricted by pain and weakness with a positive drop arm sign.
Right shoulder abduction and external rotation strength are reduced to 3/5, while bilateral elbow flexion, extension, and hand grip strength remain 5/5.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation over the right lateral shoulder deltoid patch and distal upper extremity dermatomes bilaterally.
Radial and brachial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with capillary refill under 2 seconds.
No skin rash, psoriatic plaques, tophi, or surgical scars are observed over the limbs or trunk.
Cervical spine has full range of motion without midline tenderness or radicular pain on axial compression.
